source.title: Why Ghost Outputs Teach: A Kernel-Based Understanding of Subliminal Learning
source.authors: Zhe Li; B. Ying; Chao-Sheng Dong; Hai-Bo Yang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It applies ghost-output distillation and measures downstream behavior on MNIST and a Qwen preference task, including teacher-generated unrelated outputs and controls.
record.gate_note: The teacher's cat-bias sanity check is induced by an explicit system prompt, so it is not evidence of spontaneous trait expression. The paper also discusses mechanisms theoretically; rows below record reported experimental outcomes, not cited results.
record.test_reason: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct experiment reruns the original recipe: a system-prompted cat-loving teacher, format-filtered number sequences, and a fine-tuned student scored on cat-response rate with base and control comparisons. The MNIST ghost-output ablations and the LLM input-type and hidden-state-mask sweeps test a gradient/kernel mechanism account (D).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors derive a chained cross-task NTK and argue three things: shared initialization makes the transfer operator PSD, which they call a strict prerequisite; ghost dimension is a rank bottleneck; and high-entropy inputs are broadband probes. They say MNIST experiments confirm all three and that a 7B Qwen student acquires a cat preference from numbers (91.1% vs 2.9%). Their claim that the LLM vocabulary head 'shatters' the bottleneck is theoretical only and untested.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses the related teacher-output-to-student-distillation setup, but the LLM teacher's cat preference is induced by a system prompt rather than described as a trait acquired through earlier training. The toy experiments use an MNIST ghost head; the LLM experiments use number-sequence or other prompt completions and LoRA fine-tuning.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer varies with initialization in the MLP, ghost or embedding-mask dimension, and distillation input type. In the LLM input comparison, random numbers outperform gibberish, which outperforms medical-domain prompts.
record.problems: The MNIST experiments use one small MLP; the LLM experiments use one model family. The main 2,000-response LLM rates have no reported uncertainty, and only two seeds are reported for the embedding-mask sweep. The paper does not test different base models, harmful traits, full fine-tuning, or other LoRA ranks.
record.rows_left_out: Individual points from the Figure 3a ghost-dimension sweep and Figure 4b embedding-mask sweep are not separately recorded where the text gives only a qualitative trend or grouped range; exact point values are not stated in prose.

untested.parts: Code and maths-reasoning datasets; any model family other than Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; animals other than cat.
Cross-base-model student/teacher pairs. Only a different-initialization MLP control (R3) exists, which is the original paper's MNIST analogue.
No misaligned or harmful trait is tested.
Only LoRA r=8 is used; no full fine-tuning or other ranks. The evaluation probes are the standard protocol and are not varied.

missing.what: Per-k bias rates and standard deviations for the embedding-mask sweep (k=1 to 3584). The caption says saturation beyond k≈50; the text says drops begin below k≈100.
Whether the teacher's hidden states in the mask experiment were computed with the cat system prompt present.
Task-accuracy trajectories over distillation steps for shared vs different initialization.

record.verdict_notes: Version codes V1/V4/V5 are remapped to A/D/E. The teacher is system-prompted, as in the original animal experiments, so this is not a deviation. E is dropped because the only 'robustness' evidence is the standard protocol at a single LoRA rank. The different-initialization result (R3) is an MLP analogue of B, not a cross-base-model test. Base-rate inconsistencies: 3.1% vs 3.2% base, and 14% cat for the un-prompted teacher on 50 samples vs 3.1% for the base model on 2,000. The LLM rates carry no uncertainty, and the mask sweep uses 2 seeds.

versions.untested_parts: The LLM experiments use number sequences, gibberish, and medical prompts; code and maths-reasoning datasets are not tested.
The paper compares shared with different initialization in an MLP, but does not test students and teachers with different base models.
No misalignment or other harmful alignment-relevant trait is tested.
The experiments examine backbone/head updates, ghost or embedding-mask dimension, and input type. They do not directly test token entanglement, rare divergence tokens, or a steering-vector carrier.
The effect is evaluated on animal-preference prompts distinct from training inputs, but only LoRA rank 8 is used; full fine-tuning and other LoRA ranks are not tested.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens without fine-tuning is tested.
